fields.title: Acquisition strategy: how channels build up for the year
fields.keyTakeaway: An acquisition strategy means choosing several segments and a channel portfolio for each, with clear capacity and payback period. One working channel is not a strategy, but luck with an expiration date.
fields.checkQuestion: One channel brings 80% of clients and pays off well. Why is this dangerous?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **which segments to acquire and how?** In module M2, we went through channels and calculated their unit economics; here, we look at how this builds into an annual plan when you have multiple segments.
fields.blocks/1/text: Running example: Reestr—a fictional document management service for small businesses. After fixing its funnel, the company grows and plans the year.
fields.blocks/2/title: What an acquisition strategy consists of
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Segments and sequence**—who we work with first and who we deliberately decline.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Channel portfolio**—tailored to each segment. A cheap channel is usually narrow: it has a capacity, and you need to know it.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Role of channels**—some bring customers today, others build brand awareness for the future. You cannot measure them with the same ruler.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Payback period and buffer**—how many months it takes for the product to recover customer acquisition costs and how many such cycles fit into a year.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Segment 1—sole proprietors without employees. Search by task-based queries (capacity almost maxed out, 60% of available traffic is already ours), bank partnerships—a new channel, testing it with a 300 thousand bet.

Segment 2—small companies with an accountant. Partnership with accounting services: 22 clients per quarter with zero budget, capacity not yet maxed out.

Who we reject: companies over 50 people—they require integrations we don't have, and the sales cycle is four times longer.

Role of channels: search—today; industry publications—awareness, measured not by leads, but by the share of mentions in sales calls.

Reserve: 20% of the budget to test two new channels with bets.
fields.blocks/4/text: As long as a channel works, nobody looks for a second one. When its capacity runs out or platform rules change, the company has neither alternatives nor accumulated knowledge. Build a second channel in advance, deliberately prepared for worse economics.
fields.blocks/4/title: Dependence on a single channel is the main growth risk
fields.blocks/5/text: An annual acquisition plan survives only until the first quarter of actual data: capacity turns out smaller, costs go up. It is useful to log decisions rather than lead numbers—which segments and channels we test, and at what result we stop.
